title: Embeddings: meaning as direction
summary: An embedding layer is a table with one row per token. Looking up a token's row is the same as multiplying its one-hot vector by the table, and a whole sequence becomes a (T × d) matrix. The rows start random; training pushes words used in similar contexts towards similar directions, which cosine similarity measures.
llm_link: The first layer of every GPT is an embedding table of shape (vocabulary size × d_model); GPT-2 small, for example, uses 768 numbers per token. Embeddings APIs that you have used for RAG return vectors of the same kind, read from deeper inside a model, and you compare them with cosine similarity for exactly the reason in this lesson.
key_ideas: The embedding table E has shape (V, d): V tokens in the vocabulary, d numbers per token.
Embedding a token is a row lookup, E[id]. Mathematically it is one_hot(id) @ E, which is why it counts as a layer.
A sequence of T token IDs becomes E[ids], a (T, d) matrix. T and d are the two numbers to track from now on.
The table is learned. Words that help make similar predictions get pushed towards similar directions.
Compare embeddings by direction with cosine similarity: a · b / (|a| |b|).

quiz.q: E has shape (50000, 768) and ids is an array of 12 token IDs. Predict the shape of E[ids].
quiz.explain: Indexing with an array of 12 IDs picks 12 rows, each with 768 numbers: one row per token, one column per embedding dimension.

quiz.q: Why is multiplying a one-hot vector by E the same as looking up a row?
options: Because every entry of the one-hot vector except one is zero, so every other row of E is multiplied by zero
It is only approximately the same
quiz.explain: one_hot @ E adds up the rows of E weighted by the one-hot entries. Only the row at the 1 survives, exactly.

quiz.q: Before training, the embedding rows for "cat" and "kitten" are…
options: Already close, because the words are spelled similarly
quiz.explain: The table starts with small random numbers. Similar directions appear only because training nudges rows of words used in similar contexts the same way.

quiz.q: a = [2, 0] and b = [5, 0]. What is their cosine similarity?
quiz.explain: They point in exactly the same direction, so the angle is 0 and the cosine is 1. The lengths (2 and 5) divide out.

quiz.q: In RAG you rank documents by cosine similarity between embedding vectors. What does a score near 0 suggest?
options: The texts are opposites in meaning
The vectors point in unrelated directions, so the texts are probably about different things
One text is much longer than the other
quiz.explain: Cosine measures direction only. Near 0 means roughly perpendicular: little shared meaning in the learned space. Length, which can reflect text length or word frequency, drops out.

problems.title: Shape drill: predict before you print
problems.prompt:
From now on, most bugs you will meet are shape bugs. Before running anything, predict the NumPy shape of each expression and write it as a tuple in answers. Then print the real shapes and see which ones surprised you.

Reminders: indexing a 2D array with one integer picks a row; indexing with an array of integers picks several rows; np.eye(V) is the V × V identity, so its rows are one-hot vectors; (a, b) @ (b, c) gives (a, c). A 1D shape is written with a trailing comma, like (3,).
problems.starter:
import numpy as np

V, d = 6, 4                  # vocabulary size, embedding width
E = np.zeros((V, d))         # the embedding table: one row per token
ids = np.array([0, 2, 3])    # "the cat sat" as token IDs, so T = 3

# Predict each shape as a tuple, e.g. (2, 5), WITHOUT running anything first.
# Then check yourself by printing the expression's .shape.
answers = {
    "E": None,
    "ids": None,
    "E[2]": None,
    "E[ids]": None,
    "E[ids][1]": None,
    "np.eye(V)[ids]": None,        # one-hot rows for the three tokens
    "np.eye(V)[ids] @ E": None,
}

tests.name: shape of E
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['E']
real = (E).shape
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for E'
assert tuple(got) == real, f'you predicted {got} but E has shape {real}. The table has one row per token in the vocabulary and one column per embedding dimension: (V, d).'

tests.name: shape of ids
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['ids']
real = (ids).shape
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for ids'
assert tuple(got) == real, f'you predicted {got} but ids has shape {real}. ids is a 1D array of 3 integers, and a 1D shape is written (3,).'

tests.name: shape of E[2]
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['E[2]']
real = (E[2]).shape
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for E[2]'
assert tuple(got) == real, f'you predicted {got} but E[2] has shape {real}. One integer index picks a single row, which is a 1D array of d numbers.'

tests.name: shape of E[ids]
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['E[ids]']
real = (E[ids]).shape
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for E[ids]'
assert tuple(got) == real, f'you predicted {got} but E[ids] has shape {real}. An array of T indices picks T rows, stacked: (T, d).'

tests.name: shape of E[ids][1]
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['E[ids][1]']
real = (E[ids][1]).shape
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for E[ids][1]'
assert tuple(got) == real, f'you predicted {got} but E[ids][1] has shape {real}. E[ids] is (3, 4); indexing it with 1 picks one row of 4 numbers.'

tests.name: shape of np.eye(V)[ids]
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['np.eye(V)[ids]']
real = (np.eye(V)[ids]).shape
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for np.eye(V)[ids]'
assert tuple(got) == real, f'you predicted {got} but np.eye(V)[ids] has shape {real}. Each row of np.eye(V) is a one-hot vector of length V, and we pick T of them: (T, V).'

tests.name: shape of np.eye(V)[ids] @ E
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['np.eye(V)[ids] @ E']
real = (np.eye(V)[ids] @ E).shape
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for np.eye(V)[ids] @ E'
assert tuple(got) == real, f'you predicted {got} but np.eye(V)[ids] @ E has shape {real}. (T, V) @ (V, d) gives (T, d): the inner V cancels. Same shape as E[ids], because it is the same lookup.'

hints: Write the rule (a, b) @ (b, c) -> (a, c) at the top of your page and use it.
Indexing with an array keeps one axis for the array: E[ids] has len(ids) rows.
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

V, d = 6, 4                  # vocabulary size, embedding width
E = np.zeros((V, d))         # the embedding table: one row per token
ids = np.array([0, 2, 3])    # "the cat sat" as token IDs, so T = 3

# Predict each shape as a tuple, e.g. (2, 5), WITHOUT running anything first.
# Then check yourself by printing the expression's .shape.
answers = {
    "E": (6, 4),
    "ids": (3,),
    "E[2]": (4,),
    "E[ids]": (3, 4),
    "E[ids][1]": (4,),
    "np.eye(V)[ids]": (3, 6),      # one-hot rows for the three tokens
    "np.eye(V)[ids] @ E": (3, 4),
}

problems.title: Two ways to embed a sentence

assert out.shape == (2, 4), f'expected shape (T, V) = (2, 4), got {out.shape}'

tests.name: each row sums to 1
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out = one_hot([3, 3, 1], 5)
assert np.allclose(out.sum(axis=1), 1), 'every one-hot row has exactly one 1, so each row should sum to 1'

tests.name: embed picks rows
tests.code:
import numpy as np
E = np.arange(12.0).reshape(6, 2)
out = embed(np.array([0, 2, 3]), E)
assert out is not None, 'embed returned None'
assert out.shape == (3, 2), f'expected (T, d) = (3, 2), got {np.shape(out)}'
assert np.array_equal(out, [[0, 1], [4, 5], [6, 7]]), f'expected rows 0, 2, 3 of E, got\n{out}'

tests.name: lookup equals one-hot product
tests.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
E = rng.normal(size=(10, 4))
ids = np.array([1, 7, 7, 0, 9])
a = one_hot(ids, 10) @ E
b = embed(ids, E)
assert b is not None, 'embed returned None'
assert np.allclose(a, b), 'one_hot(ids) @ E and E[ids] should be identical: the product keeps only the row where the 1 is'

hints: for t, i in enumerate(ids): out[t, i] = 1
NumPy lets you index with a whole array: E[ids]. You can also write out[np.arange(T), ids] = 1 for one_hot.

problems.title: Nearest neighbours by cosine similarity
problems.prompt:
Write most_similar(word, words, E, k): compare the row for word with every row of E using cosine similarity, and return the k most similar other words, best first.

Do it without a Python loop over rows: divide every row by its length (np.linalg.norm(E, axis=1, keepdims=True)) so all rows have length 1, and then one matrix-vector product gives every cosine at once.

words = ['cat', 'kitten', 'dog', 'car', 'truck']
most_similar('cat', words, E, 2)   # ['kitten', 'dog'] for the toy table in the tests

tests.name: finds the neighbours
tests.code:
import numpy as np
words=['cat','kitten','dog','car','truck']
E=np.array([[1.0,0.1],[0.9,0.2],[0.7,0.6],[-0.2,1.0],[-0.3,0.9]])
out=most_similar('cat',words,E,2)
assert out == ['kitten','dog'], f'expected [kitten, dog], got {out}'

tests.name: excludes the word itself
tests.code:
import numpy as np
words=['cat','kitten','dog','car','truck']
E=np.array([[1.0,0.1],[0.9,0.2],[0.7,0.6],[-0.2,1.0],[-0.3,0.9]])
out=most_similar('car',words,E,1)
assert out == ['truck'], f'a word is always most similar to itself, so skip it; expected [truck], got {out}'

tests.name: length does not matter
tests.code:
import numpy as np
words=['a','b','c']
E=np.array([[1.0,0.0],[100.0,1.0],[0.0,0.5]])
out=most_similar('c',words,E,1)
assert out == ['b'], f'b is long but its direction is closer to c than a is; cosine ignores length. Got {out}. Did you normalise the rows?'

tests.name: returns k words
tests.code:
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(1)
E=rng.normal(size=(8,5))
words=[f'w{i}' for i in range(8)]
out=most_similar('w3',words,E,4)
assert isinstance(out,list) and len(out)==4, f'expected a list of 4 words, got {out}'
assert 'w3' not in out, 'the query word should not be in its own neighbour list'

hints: En = E / np.linalg.norm(E, axis=1, keepdims=True). keepdims keeps the shape (V, 1) so the division broadcasts across each row.
order = np.argsort(-sims); return [words[j] for j in order if j != i][:k]
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def most_similar(word, words, E, k):
    En = E / np.linalg.norm(E, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    i = words.index(word)
    sims = En @ En[i]
    order = np.argsort(-sims)
    return [words[j] for j in order if j != i][:k]
